---
title: "Microkernel, Registry, and Manifest-First"
---

> A study note on how three ideas at three levels of abstraction fit together:
> an architectural **style**, a **pattern**, and a **mechanism**.

---

## 0. The map

The three concepts are often confused because they usually appear together. They
are not alternatives — they stack.

```
  ARCHITECTURAL STYLE   Microkernel / Plug-in Architecture
        |                  "thin core + independently deployable extensions"
        |
        +--------------------------------------------------+
        v                                                  v
  PATTERN               Registry                     Plugin Contract
        |                  "index of what exists"       "the interface"
        v
  MECHANISM             Manifest-first discovery
                           "populate the index from declarative data"
```

Read top-down: the style creates the need, the pattern answers it, the mechanism
implements the pattern.

---

## 1. Microkernel / Plug-in Architecture

### 1.1 Definition

A **thin core system** that provides minimal general functionality, plus a set of
**plug-in components** that supply specialized, independently deployable
behaviour. The core knows *that* plugins exist and how to talk to them; it does
not know what any specific plugin does.

```
                    +-------------------------+
                    |      CORE SYSTEM        |
                    |  (minimal, stable, thin)|
                    +------------+------------+
                                 |
        +----------+----------+--+-------+----------+
        |          |          |          |          |
   +---------+ +---------+ +---------+ +---------+ +---------+
   | Plug-in | | Plug-in | | Plug-in | | Plug-in | | Plug-in |
   |    A    | |    B    | |    C    | |    D    | |    E    |
   +---------+ +---------+ +---------+ +---------+ +---------+
   independently deployable, separately versioned, often 3rd-party
```

### 1.2 The core's three obligations

Unpack "the core" and you always find the same three jobs:

```
  +--------------------------- CORE SYSTEM ---------------------------+
  |                                                                   |
  |   +------------+    +------------+    +----------------------+    |
  |   | DISCOVERY  |--->|  REGISTRY  |--->| CONTRACT / ADAPTER   |    |
  |   |            |    |            |    |                      |    |
  |   | how do I   |    | what is    |    | how do I call it     |    |
  |   | FIND them? |    | available? |    | once I have it?      |    |
  |   +------------+    +------------+    +----------------------+    |
  |                                                                   |
  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

| Obligation | Question it answers | Typical implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Discovery | Where do plugins come from? | directory scan, config list, package index |
| Registry | What is available right now? | in-memory dict/index (Section 2) |
| Contract | How do I invoke one safely? | interface + version negotiation + adapter |

**Manifest-first (Section 3) answers Discovery, fills the Registry, and declares
one half of the Contract.**

### 1.3 Examples

| System | Core | Plug-ins |
|---|---|---|
| VS Code | editor shell | extensions |
| Quarto | render pipeline | filters, formats, extensions |
| Android | OS + framework | apps |
| Claude Code | agent loop | skills, MCP servers, hooks |
| Eclipse / OSGi | runtime | bundles |
| pytest | test runner | plugins / fixtures |
| Web browser | engine | extensions |

### 1.4 When to reach for it

```
  USE when:                          AVOID when:
  + feature set is open-ended        - feature set is small and fixed
  + third parties should extend it   - all code is yours and in-repo
  + features ship on separate        - everything ships as one binary
    schedules from the core          - the "core" would be thicker than
  + users install only what they       the plugins (no real separation)
    need
```

**Main cost:** every extension point is a public API you can no longer change
freely. Design few, wide extension points rather than many narrow ones.

---

## 2. The Registry Pattern

### 2.1 Definition

A well-known object that maps a **key** to a **thing**, so callers can look up a
component by identity or capability instead of importing it directly. It is the
core system's *memory* of what exists.

```
   Registry {
     "dicom" -> DicomReader,
     "pdf"   -> PdfExporter,
     "nifti" -> NiftiReader,
   }
   + secondary indexes: by capability, by file format, by priority
```

It is a form of **inversion of control**: the caller says *what* it needs
("a reader for `.dcm`"), not *which class* to instantiate.

### 2.2 How registries get filled — the spectrum

Registry is agnostic about its source. The options form a spectrum, and
manifest-first sits at one end:

```
 CODE-FIRST <--------------------------------------------> MANIFEST-FIRST

 (1) Manual        (2) Self-register    (3) Convention    (4) Manifest
     wiring            (decorator /         scan              file
                        static init)

 registry.add(     @register("pdf")     scan plugins/*    read plugin.yaml
   "pdf", Pdf)     class Pdf: ...       import each       import nothing
```

| | (1) Manual | (2) Decorator | (3) Scan | (4) Manifest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Must execute code to discover? | yes | yes | yes | **no** |
| Discovery cost = activation cost? | yes | yes | yes | **no** |
| Safe for untrusted plugins? | no | no | no | **yes** |
| Deterministic registration order? | yes | **no** | **no** | yes |
| Tooling / catalog friendly? | no | no | no | **yes** |
| Risk of declaration/code drift? | low | lowest | low | **higher** |

> **Import-order hazard (option 2).** A `@register` decorator never fires if
> nothing imports the module. Classic silent-failure bug in Python and in C#
> static constructors. Manifest-first eliminates it structurally: the scan is a
> directory listing, not a call graph.

### 2.3 The two-tier registry

The structural move that makes a registry manifest-first: split it, and populate
only the top tier eagerly.

```
  +-----------------------------------------------------+
  | TIER 1 -- DESCRIPTOR REGISTRY   (eager, cheap)      |
  |   key -> { metadata..., entry: "module:Class" }     |
  |   * populated by scanning manifests                 |
  |   * queryable, sortable, permission-checkable       |
  |   * NO plugin code has executed                     |
  +---------------------------+-------------------------+
                              | resolve(key)
                              v
  +-----------------------------------------------------+
  | TIER 2 -- INSTANCE REGISTRY     (lazy, expensive)   |
  |   key -> live object / factory result               |
  |   * populated on first use, then memoized           |
  +-----------------------------------------------------+
```

```python
class Registry:
    def __init__(self, root: Path):
        # Tier 1: eager, pure data -- no plugin code runs
        self._desc = {m["name"]: m for m in scan_manifests(root)}
        self._live: dict[str, object] = {}          # Tier 2: lazy

    def find(self, **query):            # query without activating
        return [d for d in self._desc.values() if matches(d, query)]

    def get(self, name):                # the ONLY door to execution
        if name not in self._live:
            d = self._desc[name]
            self._live[name] = import_string(d["entry"])()
        return self._live[name]
```

`find()` never touches plugin code. `get()` is the single activation point.
That separation is unavailable if the registry is populated by imports.

---

## 3. Manifest-First / Declarative Metadata

### 3.1 The core idea

> Describe a component's identity, capabilities, and requirements as **data** —
> separate from, and readable **before**, the code that implements it.

The manifest is the contract. The implementation is an artifact the runtime
fetches later, only if the manifest says it is needed.

```
        +-----------------------------------------+
        |  MANIFEST  (declarative, cheap, safe)   |
        |  name, version, capabilities,           |
        |  dependencies, entry point, config      |
        +--------------------+--------------------+
                             |  read + validate FIRST
                             v
        +-----------------------------------------+
        |  LOADER / RESOLVER                      |
        |  build registry, resolve deps, decide   |
        +--------------------+--------------------+
                             |  activate on demand
                             v
        +-----------------------------------------+
        |  IMPLEMENTATION (imperative, expensive) |
        |  the actual code, loaded lazily         |
        +-----------------------------------------+
```

"Manifest-**first**" is the temporal claim: nothing executes until the
description has been read and understood.

### 3.2 Side by side

**Imperative (code-first)** — to answer *"what plugins exist?"* you must import
everything:

```python
# plugins/__init__.py -- must EXECUTE to learn anything
from .pdf_export import PdfExporter
from .dicom_reader import DicomReader   # imports pydicom, numpy... 400ms

registry.register("pdf", PdfExporter)
registry.register("dicom", DicomReader)
```

**Declarative (manifest-first)** — the entry point is a *string*, not an import:

```yaml
# plugins/dicom_reader/plugin.yaml
schemaVersion: 1
name: dicom-reader
version: 1.2.0
provides: [reader]
formats: [".dcm", ".ima"]
requires: { pydicom: ">=2.4" }
entry: dicom_reader.main:DicomReader
```

```python
manifests = [yaml.safe_load(p.read_text())
             for p in Path("plugins").glob("*/plugin.yaml")]
# Everything is known. Zero plugin code has run.

chosen = next(m for m in manifests if ".dcm" in m["formats"])
cls = import_string(chosen["entry"])   # activate ONLY this one
```

### 3.3 The four properties that create the value

```
 1. INSPECTABLE WITHOUT EXECUTING
    enumerate, search, validate, permission-check, render docs,
    build a dependency graph -- without running a line

 2. LATE / LAZY BINDING
    discovery is O(read a small file); activation is deferred
    1000 plugins ~ 1000 tiny reads, 1 actual import

 3. UNIFORM SHAPE -> TOOLING
    schema-backed data enables linters, IDE completion, registries,
    reviewable diffs, codegen, marketplaces

 4. INVERSION OF CONTROL
    the component declares WHAT it is; the host decides WHEN and
    WHETHER to use it -- host owns the lifecycle
```

Property 1 is the **security** story (Android permissions, browser extension
manifests). Property 2 is the **performance** story. Property 3 is why
**ecosystems** grow around manifest-based systems.

### 3.4 The decisive argument: dependency resolution

If plugins depend on each other, you must know **all** declarations before
activating **any** of them. You cannot topologically sort a graph you are
discovering by walking it.

```
  CODE-FIRST                        MANIFEST-FIRST
  ----------                        --------------
  import A                          read all manifests
   +- A needs B?                     +- A requires B
      import B  <- discovered        +- B requires C
       +- B needs C?                 +- C requires nothing
          import C  <- discovered
             +- C needs A?          build graph -> topo-sort
                XX cycle, mid-init  -> C, B, A
                   half-built state    (or reject cleanly, nothing loaded)
```

Code-first finds the cycle *after* partially constructing objects.
Manifest-first finds it in a pure function over data, before any side effects.

This is exactly why `Cargo.toml`, `package.json` and R's `DESCRIPTION` are
separate files rather than inferred from `use` / `require` / `library()`
statements: **the resolver must run on data.**

> **Consequence:** Registry + inter-plugin dependencies => you will end up
> manifest-first whether you planned to or not.

### 3.5 Progressive disclosure — the LLM-era variant

When the scarce resource is *context window* rather than *startup time*, the
same pattern appears under a different name:

```
   ALL components       ~50 tokens each      always loaded
   +--------------------------------------+
   | name + description  (the manifest)   |  <- cheap, eager
   +--------------------------------------+
              | match / route
              v
   ONE component        ~2000 tokens        loaded on demand
   +--------------------------------------+
   | body, references/, scripts/          |  <- expensive, lazy
   +--------------------------------------+
```

Claude Code skills work this way: only YAML frontmatter (`name`,
`description`) is eagerly in context; the body is read only for the matched
skill. MCP tool schemas are the same idea for tools.

> **Rule that follows:** in a manifest-first system, **the manifest _is_ the
> interface.** A poor `description` makes an excellent skill invisible, because
> the implementation is never reached.

---

## 4. Where they meet — and where they don't

Manifest-first is a mechanism *commonly used inside* microkernel architecture,
but neither implies the other. Overlapping sets, not nesting:

```
   +---------------------------+   +---------------------------+
   | MICROKERNEL, no manifest  |   | MANIFEST-FIRST, no kernel |
   |                           |   |                           |
   | * pytest hooks            |   | * Cargo.toml / npm        |
   | * .NET MEF [Export]       |   | * Kubernetes YAML         |
   | * Emacs / vim plugins     |   | * GitHub Actions workflow |
   | * naive scan-and-import   |   | * Quarto doc frontmatter  |
   |        +------------------+---+--------------+            |
   |        |  BOTH -- the common case:           |            |
   |        |    VS Code extensions               |            |
   |        |    Android apps                     |            |
   |        |    Claude Code skills / MCP         |            |
   |        |    Quarto extensions                |            |
   |        |    OSGi bundles                     |            |
   |        +------------------+---+--------------+            |
   +---------------------------+   +---------------------------+
```

> **.NET MEF is the interesting hybrid.** `[Export]` attributes are metadata
> embedded in the assembly — declarative in spirit, but you must load the
> assembly to read them. Hence MEF's separate catalog-caching layer, which
> claws back the lazy-discovery property that a true manifest gives for free.

### 4.1 Why microkernels gravitate toward manifests

Not accidental — each defining constraint of the style pushes that way:

| Microkernel constraint | What it demands | Manifest supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Independently deployable plugins | discover without recompiling core | file scan, no imports |
| Third-party / untrusted plugins | inspect + gate before running | permissions, capabilities |
| Many available, few used | don't pay for the unused | lazy entry point |
| Core and plugins evolve apart | version negotiation | `engines`, `apiVersion` |
| Users browse and install | a marketplace needs a catalog | uniform schema |

**Canonical illustration — VS Code:** `contributes` declares every command,
menu, and setting so the UI can render them without loading anything;
`activationEvents` means the extension's JS loads only when a declared trigger
fires. Install 60 extensions, load 4.

### 4.2 Manifest layout in a plugin

```
  plugins/dicom-reader/
    plugin.yaml          <- MANIFEST: identity, deps, entry point, capabilities
    src/
      main.py            <- IMPLEMENTATION: loaded only via entry point
    tests/
```

> The manifest declares **that** the plugin satisfies a contract and **under
> what conditions** it applies. The code **proves** it.
> The interface itself (signatures, ABI) stays in code — that is the other half
> of the contract.

---

## 5. Trade-offs and failure modes

### 5.1 Manifest drift
Two sources of truth that can disagree (`entry: foo:Bar` while the code renamed
`Bar` to `Baz`). Failure surfaces at *load time* with a confusing error rather
than at compile time.
**Mitigate:** JSON-Schema validation in CI; or generate one side from the other
(decorators -> manifest, or manifest -> stub code).

### 5.2 The "YAML becomes a programming language" trap

```
   expressiveness
   needed
        |                             ,--- Helm / CI-YAML hell
        |                        ,---'
        |            ,----------'
        |     ,-----'  <- sweet spot: static facts only
        +----'------------------------------------> feature creep over time
```

Declarative formats acquire conditionals, then loops, then interpolation, then
templating — and you have built a bad language with no debugger.
**Rule:** if a field's value depends on runtime state, it does not belong in the
manifest. Add a code escape hatch instead of growing the schema.

### 5.3 Schema versioning
The manifest schema is a public API. Once third parties author manifests you
cannot rename fields. **Include `schemaVersion` from day one.**

### 5.4 Indirection cost
For a closed system with three components you own, a manifest layer is pure
ceremony.

---

## 6. Decision guide

```
  Do I need a MICROKERNEL?
    open-ended features + independent deployment + external authors  -> yes
    small fixed feature set, single binary                           -> no

  Do I need a REGISTRY?
    more than a handful of interchangeable components                -> yes
    a couple of implementations behind one interface                 -> just DI

  Do I need MANIFEST-FIRST?  (>= 2 of these)
    [ ] open set of components (plugins, 3rd-party, user-authored)
    [ ] discovery must be cheaper than activation
    [ ] components are untrusted or need permission gating
    [ ] you want tooling / a catalog / a marketplace
    [ ] non-programmers must configure or author components
    [ ] plugins depend on each other (topological ordering needed)

  Skip manifests when:
    x closed set, all in-repo, all yours
    x every component loads on every run anyway
    x the "config" is really logic in disguise
```

> **Heuristic: the manifest earns its keep at the trust boundary.**
> If plugins cross an organizational, deployment, or security boundary —
> declare. If they don't — wire them up in code and skip the ceremony.

---

## 7. One-paragraph synthesis

Microkernel is the **shape**: a thin core plus swappable extensions. Registry is
the core's **memory** of which extensions exist. Manifest-first is the
**discipline** that lets that memory be built from inert, inspectable data
instead of executed code — which in turn is what makes untrusted plugins safe,
large plugin sets fast, and inter-plugin dependencies resolvable. You can build
a microkernel without it, and many do; but every microkernel that grew a
third-party ecosystem eventually adopted it, because a marketplace is just a
registry of manifests you have not downloaded yet.

---

## Appendix — Manifest examples in the wild

| System | Manifest | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| npm | `package.json` | `node_modules/**/*.js` |
| Rust | `Cargo.toml` | `src/**/*.rs` |
| R packages | `DESCRIPTION` / `NAMESPACE` | `R/*.R` |
| Python | `pyproject.toml`, entry points | the package |
| Quarto | `_quarto.yml`, `_extension.yml` | `.qmd` body, Lua filters |
| Kubernetes | Deployment / Pod YAML | container image |
| VS Code ext. | `package.json -> contributes` | `extension.js` (lazy) |
| Android | `AndroidManifest.xml` | `classes.dex` |
| Claude Code skills | `SKILL.md` frontmatter | body + `scripts/` |
| MCP | tool JSON schemas | server handlers |
| GitHub Actions | `action.yml` | the action's code |

## Appendix — Related patterns

| Pattern | Relationship |
|---|---|
| Registry | The in-memory index the manifest populates (Section 2) |
| Service Locator | A registry queried by service type; same IoC family |
| Dependency Injection | Solves the same wiring problem from the opposite direction — the container pushes dependencies in, rather than components pulling from an index |
| Abstract Factory | Often what a registry entry *resolves to* |
| Lazy Loading / Virtual Proxy | The activation half of manifest-first |
| Progressive Disclosure | The context-window variant (Section 3.5) |
| Convention over Configuration | The competing philosophy: infer from structure instead of declaring |
